summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults was decriminalised on 16 May 1991 under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, and no source records a prosecution risk for a visitor on that basis. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold.

Marriage and civil unions are not available to same-sex couples. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and maritime marriage law provides that a marriage is void if contracted between two men or two women. In 2011 the then Minister of State Zhivargo Laing described such a marriage as void and called this a community standard. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie said in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between a male and a female determined at birth. The 2016 equality referendum bills excluded transgender and intersex people and framed marriage eligibility in the same birth-sex terms.

No national law protects transgender people from discrimination. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity, and there are no national hate-crime laws. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and no HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not treat sexual orientation as deserving protection, and attempts to include it in a proposed constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. A clause in the 2001 Employment Bill that would have banned workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation was removed shortly after passage. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data.

Hostility toward transgender people has been voiced by officeholders. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas", urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island so that "they stay out of the way", and pledged $1,000 toward the relocation.

Violence against LGBT people at tourist events is documented. In May 2017 Adrian Brown, a 24-year-old Jamaica-born visitor resident in the United States, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival because he is gay; he sought charges. The courts have accepted defences that treat a victim's homosexuality as provocation: a defendant was acquitted in 2009 of murdering a homosexual HIV-positive man using a "gay panic" defence, and on 10 June 2010 the president of the Court of Appeal stated that "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act." Killings of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved, including the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying, in which the accused was found not guilty.

Police enforcement has targeted LGBT social gatherings. Officers raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 and made no arrests because no crime had been committed; guests demanded an apology and the Ministry of Tourism apologised to the cruise company involved.

Public opinion is strongly adverse. A 2015 survey recorded 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage against 10.6% approving, and a 2013 survey recorded more than 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician against 12% positive. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations that treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been reluctant to support LGBT-rights legislation publicly. No exclusively gay bars or clubs operate; the Nassau scene is underground and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden.

Some protective machinery exists. In May 1998 the National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, prison service and police do not discriminate, and there is no prohibition on LGBT citizens serving in those forces. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference, a provision that does not name gender identity. In 2016 Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the "Bahamian Trans Lives Matter" campaign, stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians; its member Torri Culmer campaigns against the termination of transgender and intersex workers.
tangentialFactors:
The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, a decision the government overruled.

LGBT tourist groups have drawn organised protest. Church groups opposed Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise, a 1998 protest targeted a lesbian cruise, and in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a cable company's request to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo.

In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source records how Bahamian immigration or border officers treat a trans traveller whose documents or appearance differ from the sex recorded at birth, and no marker, screening or secondary-inspection practice at ports of entry is documented.

No source records bathroom, changing-room or other facility-access rules, or any enforcement of them.

Violence data in the sources concern gay men and are not disaggregated for transgender victims. No count of trans-specific incidents in the Bahamas is available, and the unsolved killings between 2001 and 2015 are not broken down by victim identity beyond the description of the victims as homosexual men.

Whether the 18-year age of consent for same-sex acts has been enforced against visitors is not documented.

Whether URCA has issued any code of practice under the Communications Act 2009 protecting LGBT people is not recorded.
